class.name: JarBodyAtmosphere
class.brief_description: A physically based atmosphere around a round body, which also lights the scene.
class.description: A smooth spherical atmosphere after Hillaire ("A Scalable and Production Ready Sky and Atmosphere Rendering Technique", 2020): Rayleigh scattering (blue sky, orange and red sunsets), Mie scattering (haze, the glow around the sun), ozone absorption (deep blue twilight) and multiple scattering (twilight and the edge of the night side are not black). Transmittance and multiple scattering are precomputed on the CPU whenever the air or the planet changes (a few milliseconds); the shader then marches each view ray once. Seen from the ground: the sky, and haze over distant terrain, which also fades towards blue (per color); from space: the glowing rim. Drawn after other transparent objects, so water and clouds get hazed too. Hidden on flat bodies. While the camera is inside it, it lights the scene: the light of a [JarBodyLight] star reaches the camera through it (reddening as the sun goes down, none behind the planet), balanced so that the sun overhead keeps the light's own color; and the [Environment]'s ambient light becomes its own ambient light (starlight, say) plus the sky's light, as bright as the sky is drawn. Heights are fractions of the atmosphere's [member thickness], so the same air works on a planet of any size. The physics are set here; the look (brightness, quality) on [member material].

method.name: contains
method.description: Whether [param global_position] is inside the atmosphere.

method.name: get_active_material
method.description: The material in use: [member material] or the default.

method.name: get_noon_sunlight
method.description: The fraction of sunlight left at sea level with the sun overhead. Star lights are balanced to it.

method.name: get_sunlight_at
method.description: The fraction of sunlight left at [param global_position] for a star in [param direction], per color: white above the atmosphere, reddened through it, black behind the planet.

members.member: Scales the sky's light added to the [Environment]'s ambient light while the camera is inside the atmosphere.
How much light the ground reflects back up into the air (multiple scattering).

The atmosphere's look ([code]sun_intensity[/code], quality). Empty: the default [code]atmosphere.gdshader[/code]. A first pass ([code]atmosphere_extinction.gdshader[/code]) dims what is behind before it.
How strongly haze scatters forward: higher makes a tighter, brighter glow around the sun.
Vertical optical depth of the haze (Mie scattering).
Height over which the haze thins out to 1/e, as a fraction of [member thickness].
Vertical optical depth of the ozone layer per color (absorption): it keeps the twilight sky blue.
Height of the ozone layer's peak, as a fraction of [member thickness].
Full width of the ozone layer, as a fraction of [member thickness].
Vertical optical depth of the air per color (red, green, blue): how much light it scatters between the ground and space. Earth's is about (0.05, 0.11, 0.27).

Height over which the air thins out to 1/e, as a fraction of [member thickness]. Earth has about 0.1; a game planet is so small that everything in view is far in atmospheric terms, so a gentler profile keeps nearby terrain clear.

The air counts this many times over for sunlight on its way in (not on the way to the camera). On a small planet sunlight crosses little air even at the horizon, so sunsets would be pale; this makes them orange and red (and the sky and terrain they light) without hazing nearby terrain. 1: physical.
Height of the atmosphere as a fraction of the sea level radius.
